articles.text: Figure caption, Watch: William and Catherine walk green carpet in Mumbai for Earthshot Prize By Alex Boyd Published 17 November 2026, 17:25 GMT Updated 40 minutes ago The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize. Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects. One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population. Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley. The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers. Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally. They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion. Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing. During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them. He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale". Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis. The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow. "The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come." Image source, Press Association Image caption, William and Catherine talk with guests during the awards ceremony in Mumbai Image source, Press Association Image caption, The royal couple also spoke to those performing, which included Take That There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-Free World; and Fix Our Climate. Five winners were chosen from a list of 15 finalists who attended Tuesday's awards ceremony. Earthshot Prize 2026 - full list of winners Protect and Restore Nature: Bhutan, the country that helps to protect the water security of 1.6 billion people across South Asia and has a national nature coalition that aims to revive forests and rivers by restoring 50,000 hectares of damaged land Build a Waste-Free World: PFAS-Free France, a national campaign that helped secure landmark legislation banning 'forever chemicals' in France by 2030, and hopes to extend the ban to more major countries Revive Our Oceans: Niue Ocean Wide Trust, the Pacific island's scheme that has safeguarded marine life by investing in conservation to fund the long-term protection of its vast waters Clean Our Air: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a scheme rolling out up to one million electric rickshaws across India with the aim to drasitically cut one of the world's largest sources of on-road air pollution Fix Our Climate: Ørsted, a global energy company that has cut its direct carbon emissions by more than 98% by transforming from being highly coal-intensive to a leader in offshore wind Image source, EPA Image caption, Indian actor Sonam Kapoor was among the famous guests invited to attend the annual awards night Image source, EPA Image caption, Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar (right) also appeared alongside his wife Anjali (second right), daughter Sara (second left) and daughter-in-law Saaniya (left) The Earthshot prize, first held in 2020, was inspired by former US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely. Tuesday's event also saw appearances on stage from Earthshot ambassadors Robert Irwin, the Australian conservationist, and Nomzamo Mbatha, the South African actor. As well as Take That, there were also musical performances from a number of Indian artists including Shreya Ghoshal, composer and pianist Merlin D'Souza and all-female hip hop collective Wild Wild Women. The dazzling awards night was brought to a close by musician and composer Shashwat Sachdev. Image source, Press Association Image caption, After driving an electric rickshaw, William said he would've liked a longer promenade so he could "see what the top speed was" Earlier on Tuesday, William and Catherine drove in an electric rickshaw to meet the 15 finalists. As William stepped from the vehicle, which is manufactured by prize winner Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and has a top speed of 55mph, he said: "It was quite good fun, really good fun." The couple arrived in India on Monday for the three-day visit, which is expected to also include a meeting with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday. Their first engagement saw them play a game of street - or "gully" cricket - in Mumbai alongside Tendulkar. Related topics UK Royal Family Environment Asia Mumbai

articles.text: Image caption, The contaminated Mobuoy dump is thought to cover more than 100 acres of land By Mike McBride and Davy Wilson , BBC News NI Published 9 hours ago More than £160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said. The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres. Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation. Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of £161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period. Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site". He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility. Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor. Image source, PA Media Image caption, Andrew Muir says it could take a generation to clean up the Mobuoy dump in County Londonderry Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally. The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it. The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches. 'Road map for remediation' "This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, . The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency. "One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after." Image caption, The site, located on the outskirts of the city, is a former recycling plant Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved. "I want to finish this mandate with a degree of certainty for the local community, so we have a road map here for remediation," he said. "I am pushing ahead with real enthusiasm with this." Muir said the drinking water was tested regularly to ensure it was safe and that he would continue to work with all agencies to provide the local community with greater assurances about the site. Muir said the Mobuoy site remained in private ownership, but they were "actively" considering ways of transferring it. One option is vesting, which allows government departments to obtain compulsory and legal ownership of land through a court order.
